name: Downy mildew
summary: A foliar oomycete disease of Cannabis. Angular chlorotic-to-brown lesions and dark underside sporulation are stronger clues than top-surface discoloration alone.
affectedParts: older inner-canopy leaves first in documented field observations
lower leaf surface directly beneath lesions
younger and upper-canopy leaves as disease progresses
inflorescences in the New York field report
indicators: Early upper-surface lesions are yellow-green or reddish-brown, irregular, and may carry an uneven light-green or yellow halo.
Expanding lesions become brown, angular or elongated, and visibly bounded by leaf veins rather than remaining uniformly circular.
Corresponding lower-surface lesions can bear purplish-gray to gray-black down-like sporulation during wet, humid periods.
Underside sporulation can be transient: Ontario field guidance reports it most often in the morning before wind dispersal, so a midday absence is weak negative evidence.
Documented field distribution began on older leaves in the humid inner canopy and moved upward as disease progressed.
Heavily lesioned leaves can distort, curl, necrose, and fall, producing progressive lower- or inner-canopy thinning.
Multiple cultivars were affected in the New York field report, but a 108-entry assay showed susceptibility from 0 to 100%, so severity and visibility are genotype-dependent.
Leaves and inflorescences were affected in the New York report; Ontario observations found no flower or seed-head injury in that outbreak, so floral involvement is possible but not required.
exclusions: White superficial colonies on either leaf surface, especially if they wipe or scrape away, fit powdery mildew better than downy mildew.
Black pepper-like pycnidia embedded in lesions support Septoria rather than Pseudoperonospora.
Orange underside pustules or spores support rust rather than gray-black downy-mildew sporulation.
Lower-surface sooty material identified as Pseudocercospora conidiophores and conidia excludes a Pseudoperonospora species label for that sampled lesion.
A uniform exposure-edge, spray-track, droplet, or contact pattern with no organism evidence supports chemical or physical injury.
General interveinal chlorosis without discrete vein-bounded lesions or corresponding underside signs supports a nutrient or root-zone differential.
Mites, thrips, frass, residue, or necrotic tissue explain the dark underside material under magnification.
A negative midday underside photograph does not exclude downy mildew; repeat the inspection while leaves are wet and before early-morning sporulation disperses.

progression.description: Small yellow-green to reddish-brown irregular spots appear, often on older leaves within a humid closed canopy.
Spots enlarge, develop irregular yellow halos, and become angular or elongated where veins constrain the lesion.
Purplish-gray to gray-black down-like growth appears on the lower surface directly beneath lesions during wet, humid periods, often most visibly in the early morning.
New lesions move upward from older inner-canopy leaves; repeated matched captures should show whether the distribution expands beyond the original humidity pocket.
Lesions coalesce, leaves deform or curl, necrosis increases, and defoliation reduces healthy canopy; the timing and severity vary strongly among genotypes and assay conditions.

lookAlikes: Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot
Two-spotted spider mite or thrips injury
confirmation: Capture the same attached lesion from the upper surface and directly corresponding lower surface, plus whole-plant and canopy-location context; include a scale, leaf age, crop stage, and whether veins bound the lesion.
Inspect before the first winds of the day while leaves are still wet or humid, then repeat after drying to document whether underside fuzz was transient; do not treat a midday negative as definitive.
Use a hand lens or microscope to separate branching sporangiophores and sporangia from pycnidia, conidia, rust pustules, insects, frass, residue, and necrotic tissue.

Submit multiple actively developing, plant-linked lesions with matched upper/lower images and collection metadata to a plant diagnostic laboratory; preserve several asymptomatic comparison leaves from the same area.
Confirm Pseudoperonospora cannabina with oomycete morphology plus validated molecular evidence; the New York report used ITS, cox2, and ypt1 and confirmed a reisolate after pathogenicity testing.

Retain cultivar, assay type, tissue type, inoculation or field context, time of day, humidity or leaf wetness, and sampling location with every image label because these factors change symptom visibility and severity estimates.

Keep symptom-only, upper-surface-only, midday-underside-only, detached-stock-photo, mixed-pathogen, unlinked-laboratory, low-resolution, forum, vendor, or generated captures out of the confirmed downy-mildew class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Photograph distribution and matched leaf surfaces before disturbing the canopy, preferably during the early-morning sporulation window.
Separate heavily symptomatic material where operationally appropriate, preserve fresh diagnostic samples, and avoid moving wet symptomatic foliage through unaffected areas.
Record recent dew, rainfall, irrigation, leaf-wetness duration, canopy closure, airflow, cultivar, and whether symptoms cluster in older humid inner-canopy leaves.
correctivePlan: Base disease-management decisions on a confirmed oomycete diagnosis and products or practices legally permitted for the crop, jurisdiction, and production setting.
Reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness and improve foliage drying or airflow where feasible, while recognizing that an environmental response does not retroactively confirm the pathogen.
Mark lesions and repeat upper/lower/canopy captures to distinguish new infection, transient sporulation, lesion aging, and leaf loss.
prevention: Scout older inner-canopy leaves and their undersides as canopies close, with extra attention after extended dew, rain, misting, or other leaf-wetness periods.
Maintain sanitation and airflow practices that limit prolonged canopy humidity and avoid unnecessary wetting of foliage.
Keep cultivar identity and source-lot metadata because the controlled germplasm study documented extreme susceptibility differences.
warnings: Pseudoperonospora is an oomycete, not a true fungus; a generic mildew label can lead to incorrect organism and management assumptions.
Vein-limited brown lesions, yellow halos, and underside dark growth overlap other pathogens and injuries and do not establish species without plant-linked organism evidence.
Underside sporulation may be absent by midday, after drying, or in a single frame; time of day and wetness must accompany negative observations.
The 2026 resistance study used leaf-disc, detached-leaf, visual, and CNN phenotyping methods that produced different severity estimates; those scores are not universal production-image thresholds.
Field reports disagree on whether reproductive tissue is visibly affected, so flower or seed-head involvement is neither required nor safe to infer from foliar severity.
The two Ontario photographs are credited but lack explicit reusable or automated-training rights. They remain metadata-only, hidden from display, and training-prohibited; no media file is copied.
No photo or video is ground truth without linked sampling and organism confirmation; all symptom-only, rights-unclear, mixed-organism, and low-resolution samples require human review.

sources.title: First Report of Downy Mildew Caused by Pseudoperonospora cannabina on Cannabis sativa in New York
supportedClaims: In an August 2020 Ithaca, New York field trial, downy-mildew-like symptoms affected leaves and inflorescences of multiple hemp cultivars, including Auto CBD.
ITS and cox2 sequences were 100% identical to Pseudoperonospora cannabina references and ypt1 was 97.95% identical; the representative isolate was deposited as CUP-070922.

Whole-plant pathogenicity testing used ten four-week-old Anka plants and water controls; sporangia and the previously described symptoms occurred seven days after inoculation, controls remained asymptomatic, and the reisolate was confirmed by morphology plus ITS, cox2, and ypt1 sequencing.

The New York report establishes Pseudoperonospora cannabina as a causal oomycete on Cannabis, but field symptoms or dark underside material alone are not equivalent to its morpho-molecular confirmation.

sources.title: Evaluation of downy mildew resistance in the USDA Hemp Germplasm Repository using high-throughput and traditional phenotyping methods
supportedClaims: Pseudoperonospora cannabina causes angular brown foliar lesions and dark sporulation on leaf undersides and can be associated with leaf curling, defoliation, and yield loss.
The study evaluated 108 hemp entries by robotic convolutional-neural-network leaf-disc analysis, visual scoring of the same discs, and detached-leaf assays; susceptibility ranged from 0 to 100%.

G 33532 and Santhica 27 had 0% severity across all three methods, while detached-leaf, CNN, and visual methods produced systematically different severity estimates; cultivar and assay context must therefore remain attached to image labels.
The CNN method consistently underestimated severity relative to visual assessment, so experimental machine scores are not a universal field or production-image threshold.

sources.title: Foliar Diseases of Outdoor Hemp (Cannabis sativa) and Their Management 2021
sources.publisher: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs
supportedClaims: In Ontario field hemp, downy mildew risk increased as canopies closed, humidity accumulated in the canopy center, and extended leaf wetness occurred.
Symptoms began as small reddish-brown irregular spots with irregular yellow halos, expanded into roughly circular patches, and became elongated and confined by leaf veins.

Purplish-gray fuzz could appear on the lower surface beneath lesions in the morning and disappear after spores dispersed in the first winds of the day, making capture time a critical negative-evidence limitation.
Unlike Septoria lesions, the documented downy-mildew lesions lacked black pycnidia; unlike powdery mildew, the causal organism is an oomycete rather than a surface-growing fungus.

Figures 4 and 5 are Cannabis symptom photographs credited to Amy Fang Shi, OGGA, but the page states no reusable image or automated-training license; they are indexed only as rights-restricted reference metadata.

sources.title: Most Prevalent Diseases
supportedClaims: Purdue describes upper-surface yellow-green spots that become angular and brown, with heavily lesioned leaves becoming distorted and plants defoliating.
Gray-to-black down-like growth on corresponding leaf undersides during wet periods is a crucial sign, while chemical damage and other leaf spots are important visual confounders.
High humidity and free water on leaves are conducive conditions; environmental context supports a differential but does not confirm the organism.
The institutional page lists images but retains Purdue copyright and does not state item-level reusable or automated-training terms, so no Purdue media were copied or admitted.
